issues.description: The Methods section explicitly states a final sample size of N = 372, but every table in the manuscript reports N = 321 (Tables 1 and 2) or N = 244 (Table 3). The unexplained discrepancy of 51 participants between the text and the tables means readers cannot determine which sample was actually used for the main hypothesis tests, nor can the analyses be replicated. No explanation is provided for this discrepancy anywhere in the manuscript.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372. [vs.] Note. N = 321.

issues.description: The correlation between T4 Compassion Fatigue and T4 Enacted Incivility is r = .94, which is actually higher than the reliability of the enacted incivility scale (α = .91). Many other inter-construct correlations are similarly extreme: T3 Negative Emotions and T4 Enacted Incivility = .87; T3 Negative Emotions and T4 Compassion Fatigue = .86; T1 Compassion Fatigue and T1 Enacted Incivility = .85. Correlations at or above scale reliability indicate that the constructs are empirically indistinguishable, and confirmatory factor analysis fit indices (CFI, TLI) can remain high even when discriminant validity has failed. This severely undermines the serial mediation model, which depends on these being distinct constructs linked in a causal sequence.
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue [and] T4 Enacted Incivility [correlation =] .94 [with T4 Enacted Incivility alpha =] .91

issues.description: The final mediator (Compassion Fatigue) and the outcome variable (Enacted Incivility) are both measured at Time 4. This violates the fundamental requirement for causal mediation inference: the mediator must temporally precede the outcome. When two variables are measured simultaneously, it is impossible to determine which causes which, or whether both are caused by a third variable. Accordingly, the final step of the serial mediation (Compassion Fatigue → Enacted Incivility) cannot support causal conclusions, undermining the central claim of Hypothesis 4.
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue [and] T4 Enacted Incivility [both listed as T4 in Table 2 and Table 3]

issues.description: The direct effect of T2 Customer Incivility on T4 Enacted Incivility is negative and non-significant (B = -.07, SE = .05, t = -1.14, p = .40 in Table 2; B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40 in the supplemental analysis), while the indirect effect is positive and significant (B = .06). A negative direct effect combined with a positive indirect effect is a classic suppression pattern, meaning the total effect of experienced incivility on enacted incivility is approximately zero (-.07 + .06 ≈ -.01). This fundamentally contradicts the paper's thesis that incivility begets incivility, yet the authors describe this as a straightforward mediation finding without acknowledging the sign reversal or near-zero total effect.
issues.quote: T2 Customer Incivility [to T4 Enacted Incivility] B = -.07, SE = .05, t = -1.14 [non-significant direct effect, vs.] indirect... B = .06** [positive and significant]

issues.description: The Discussion characterizes the results as supporting 'a partial mediation process.' However, partial mediation requires a significant direct effect alongside the indirect effect. Here, the direct effect of T2 customer incivility on T4 enacted incivility is non-significant (p = .40), which by conventional criteria indicates full mediation—not partial. More accurately, the sign reversal between direct (negative) and indirect (positive) paths qualifies this as inconsistent mediation or suppression, which has a different theoretical interpretation. Calling this 'partial mediation' is incorrect and overstates the support for the experienced-to-enacted incivility relationship.
issues.quote: Our results support a partial mediation process: in support of our hypotheses, experiencing incivility from patients was related to increased future incivility enactment towards patients indirectly through increased negative emotions towards patients and compassion fatigue.

issues.description: The indirect effect for Hypothesis 4 is reported in the text as B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]. However, Table 2 reports the same indirect effect as B = .06, SE = .02, t = 2.58, p < .01. The CI half-width of .04 is consistent with SE = .02 (not SE = .04). If the true SE were .04, the z-ratio would be 1.5 (p ≈ .13), rendering the effect non-significant. One of these values is incorrect, and the discrepancy changes whether the hypothesis is supported.
issues.quote: Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]). [vs. Table 2:] B = .06, SE = .02, t = 2.58

issues.description: The paper explicitly states it utilizes 'social learning theory (Bandura, 1977)' as a theoretical framework, but the description that follows does not describe social learning theory. Social learning theory posits that behavior is acquired through observation and modeling of others. Instead, the text describes the stressor-emotion model (Spector & Fox, 2005): 'enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions.' These are distinct mechanisms and distinct theories; conflating them undermines the conceptual clarity of the paper.
issues.quote: we utilize social learning theory (Bandura, 1977). This model considers how individuals learn behaviors through observation and modeling of others' actions... Applied to enacted incivility, the general premise of the model suggests that enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions (Spector & Fox, 2005).

issues.description: The CFA for discriminant validity was conducted only on Time 1 variables ('absent of the temporal control measures'). With four waves of repeated-measures data, establishing that the same factor structure, loadings, and intercepts hold across waves (configural, metric, and scalar invariance) is a necessary precondition for meaningful longitudinal comparisons. Without invariance testing, observed mean-level changes or between-wave relationships could reflect changes in how constructs are measured rather than true changes in the constructs themselves.
issues.quote: we assessed our hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures... The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99

issues.subcategory: missing data treated with listwise deletion
issues.description: The patient acuity moderator has substantial missing data, causing the sample to drop from N = 321 in the main analyses to N = 244 in moderation models—a 24% reduction. The authors use listwise deletion rather than modern missing-data techniques such as multiple imputation or full information maximum likelihood (FIML). The fact that 45% of missing values resulted from out-of-range entries (not just non-response) suggests the data may not be missing at random, further biasing the listwise-deleted estimates. No missing-data analysis or sensitivity check is reported.
issues.quote: Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response)... Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.subcategory: indirect effect formula error for serial mediation
issues.description: For the serial mediation in Hypothesis 4 (X → M1 → M2 → Y), the total indirect effect requires multiplying three path coefficients: the path from X to M1, from M1 to M2, and from M2 to Y. The authors state 'the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).' This description omits one of the three required paths. With the path-labeling convention used in Hypothesis 2 (a = X→M1, d = M1→M2), the remaining M2→Y path is completely absent from the formula, making the reported calculation mathematically incorrect for a two-mediator serial mediation.
issues.quote: the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).

issues.description: The methods state 78 people were excluded for data quality, but the two described criteria account for only 57 people: inconsistent demographics (n = 56) and excessive missing values (n = 1). The remaining 21 excluded participants are never explained. Additionally, the arithmetic for the final sample is off: 468 (T1) − 16 (missing waves) − 78 (data quality) = 374, not the reported N = 372. The combination of these numerical inconsistencies makes the sample composition impossible to verify.
issues.quote: whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality)... (a) demographic information was not consistent... (n = 56)... (b) missing values exceeded 50%... (n = 1). This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent coefficients across tables for same path
issues.description: The path from T2 Customer Incivility to T4 Enacted Incivility is reported as B = -.07 (non-significant, p = .40) in Table 2 but B = .17 (significant, p < .01) in Table 3. This sign reversal on a central path in the model—from negative to positive, and from non-significant to significant—is never discussed. While different sample sizes (N = 321 vs. N = 244) or model specifications could contribute to some variation, a sign reversal on a key hypothesis-related path requires explicit explanation and has major implications for interpretation.
issues.quote: T2 Customer Incivility [→ T4 Enacted Incivility]: B = -.07, SE = .05, t = -1.14 [Table 2] vs. B = .17**, SE = .07, t = 2.67 [Table 3]

issues.description: In the supplemental relative importance analysis, both compassion fatigue and negative emotions have identical unstandardized regression coefficients (B = .23, SE = .04) predicting enacted incivility. Yet the relative importance analysis assigns them very different proportions of explained variance (45.1% vs. 30.8%). Identical regression coefficients in the same model do not typically produce such disparate relative importance metrics without a specific mathematical reason (e.g., differing intercorrelations with other predictors), which is not explained. Additionally, the coefficient for compassion fatigue in the supplemental analysis (B = .23) contradicts Table 2 (B = .57) without explanation.
issues.quote: compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001)... negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001)... compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.subcategory: control variables omitted from regression tables
issues.description: The analytic strategy and Table 1 title indicate that Time 1 values of all constructs serve as controls, yet Tables 2 and 3 do not display T1 control variables or their coefficients. Without reporting these control parameters, readers cannot evaluate whether the T1 autoregressive effects are adequately handled, whether they are significant, or how their inclusion affects the pattern of results. This omission also makes full replication of the analyses impossible.
issues.quote: This allowed us to assess the covariances between all variables (including controls) within each wave (Liu et al., 2016). [Table 1 title:] Correlation and Descriptive Information for Hypothesized Model with Time 1 Controls

issues.description: Recruitment relied entirely on personal networks, social media, and flyer distribution. Critically, one channel was 'a support group for midwest ICU nurses on Facebook,' which targets nurses already seeking peer support—likely those experiencing elevated stress, burnout, or incivility. This self-selection systematically biases the sample toward higher levels of the key study constructs, inflating prevalence estimates and potentially the observed correlations, while limiting generalizability.
issues.quote: nurse/healthcare specific forums or groups within social media networks (e.g., support group for midwest ICU nurses on Facebook)

issues.subcategory: study window mismatched to construct timescale
issues.description: Compassion fatigue is theoretically conceptualized as a progressive, cumulative condition requiring 'prolonged, continuous, and intense contact with customers.' Treating week-to-week changes in a four-week window as the temporal unit of analysis for a construct explicitly defined by prolonged accumulation is a temporal validity problem. Weekly fluctuations in compassion fatigue scores within a month may reflect transient mood states rather than the chronic, structural burnout the construct is meant to capture.
issues.quote: Both components of compassion fatigue are progressive and cumulative and can lead to severe work and health-related outcomes... [Data were collected] once per week for four weeks

issues.description: The study presents multiple formal hypotheses but no mention of pre-registration is made. The supplemental analyses—including the conditional indirect effect and the relative importance analysis—are explicitly described as 'unhypothesized,' raising concerns about post-hoc hypothesis generation (HARKing) and selective reporting. Without a pre-registered analysis plan, it is impossible for readers to distinguish confirmatory from exploratory findings.
issues.quote: Supplemental analyses. We conducted a series of supplemental analyses to 1) address unhypothesized moderation effects and 2) investigate the relationship between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility.

issues.description: Nurses self-reporting how often they were rude, condescending, or dismissive toward patients is particularly susceptible to social desirability bias, as these behaviors are professionally prohibited and ethically serious in healthcare. The pilot finding that 90% of respondents endorsed having engaged in these behaviors is ambiguous: it could mean the items are benign enough to escape social desirability suppression, or it could indicate response inflation in an anonymous survey context. Either way, the validity of self-reported enacted incivility toward vulnerable patients has not been established with objective or multi-rater methods.
issues.quote: 90% of respondents indicated that they personally had engaged in these behaviors towards patients or their families.

issues.subcategory: anomalous negative correlation between work hours and incivility unexplained
issues.description: Work hours exhibits a consistently strong and counterintuitive negative correlation with all incivility and affect variables across time points (e.g., T1 Work Hours with T1 Customer Incivility = -.39; with T1 Negative Emotions = -.38; with T3 Negative Emotions = -.44). This implies that nurses working fewer hours experience more incivility and greater emotional strain, the opposite of what workload theories would predict. This pattern is never discussed and may reflect a confound such as employment status, shift type, or seniority. It also raises questions about the role of work hours as a control variable.
issues.quote: T1 Work Hours [correlated with] T1 Customer Incivility: -.39; T1 Negative Emotions: -.38; T1 Compassion Fatigue: -.38; T1 Enacted Incivility: -.38

issues.subcategory: external validity of enacted incivility construct in high-acuity settings
issues.description: The study deliberately targets high-stakes care settings (ICUs, emergency departments, operating rooms) where many patients may be sedated, unconscious, intubated, or otherwise unable to perceive interpersonal rudeness. Items like 'put down one or more patients/patient family members or acted condescendingly toward them' conflate behaviors directed at patients versus family members without distinction, and the construct's applicability to critically ill, non-responsive patients is not addressed.
issues.quote: high-stakes nursing settings (e.g., emergency departments, intensive care units, operating rooms)... 'Put down one or more patients/patient family members or acted condescendingly towards them'

issues.subcategory: high cross-wave correlations not adequately addressed
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that 'some of the bivariate relationships are higher than convention' and attribute this to the within-person design characteristic of diary studies—but this study is not a diary study. It uses weekly panel surveys, not multiple daily assessments. The proposed remedy (centering variables on the individual mean in a multilevel framework) addresses within-person diary variance inflation but is not applicable to this design. The extremely high cross-wave correlations (e.g., T2 Customer Incivility with T3 Negative Emotions = .83; T2 Customer Incivility with T4 Compassion Fatigue = .85) are more consistent with common method variance or discriminant validity failure than diary design artifacts.
issues.quote: We acknowledge this particular issue in this study as some of the bivariate relationships are higher than convention. Future researchers may address this particular issue by integrating a latent multilevel framework that reduces potential serial and inflation effects by employing a within design that centers variables on the individual mean.

issues.description: Participants who missed any single wave were permanently excluded from all subsequent waves, ensuring that only the most compliant (or least burdened) nurses remain in the final sample. This design choice, combined with the extreme retention rates reported (98% per wave), suggests either substantial demand characteristics or that dropout occurred primarily among nurses too overworked or distressed to complete surveys—precisely the population most relevant to the study's questions. The authors' claim of comparability between completers and dropouts is based only on T1 scale means within one SD, which is not a formal missing-data analysis.
issues.quote: Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys... Participants who responded only to the T1 survey reported similar demographic information compared to those who completed all four time periods and had scale values on the key study constructs within one standard deviation of the means

issues.subcategory: citation year error and author name misspelling
issues.description: The literature review cites 'Arnold & Walsh, 2005' but the reference list contains only 'Arnold & Walsh, 2015'—either the in-text year is wrong or the 2005 reference is missing entirely. Additionally, the same author is cited as both 'Grandy et al., 2007' and 'Grandey et al., 2007' within the same paragraph of the introduction; the reference list confirms the correct spelling is Grandey.
issues.quote: Arnold & Walsh, 2005... Grandy et al., 2007... Grandey et al., 2007

issues.subcategory: CFA fit statistics formatting and interpretation
issues.description: The chi-square symbol is missing from the fit statistics report, rendering the chi-square value unidentifiable ('(269) = 862.05'). More substantively, an RMSEA of .08 is at the upper boundary of what is considered acceptable (with many methodologists recommending .06 as a cutoff for good fit and .08 for adequate fit), but the authors describe this without qualification as 'acceptable.' Given the discriminant validity concerns raised by extremely high inter-construct correlations, a more cautious characterization of fit is warranted.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99

issues.description: The quantitative pilot study to validate the shortened scales was conducted on n = 50 nurses recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk. MTurk nurses may differ systematically from hospital bedside nurses in work context, employment status, experience level, and motivation. Part-whole correlations from a MTurk nursing sample may not accurately reflect those that would be found in the target population of critical-care hospital nurses, limiting the validity evidence for the shortened scales.
issues.quote: The quantitative pilot consisted of n = 50 nurses who worked in high-stakes settings and were recruited from MTurk.
